title: Prerequisites
content:
This chapter prepares everything you need before deploying shop-ai: an AWS account, the tools on your machine, the source code, CDK bootstrap, budget alerts and the HMAC key. It ends with the expected cost, estimated with AWS Pricing Calculator and compared with the team’s real bill.
Goals Your machine has the right tool versions and can sign in to AWS from the CLI. Your AWS account is CDK-bootstrapped in ap-southeast-1 and has budgets that email you when spending passes a threshold. An HMAC key exists in Parameter Store, so recommendations work right after the deploy. You know how much this lab costs, and how much a month of real use costs. 5.2.1. AWS account An AWS account. Use a separate account for the lab, not one that runs real workloads. An IAM user or role with administrator access (AdministratorAccess). CDK creates IAM roles, CloudFormation stacks, Lambda, DynamoDB, S3, CloudFront, Cognito, SQS and SNS. Lab Region: Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1. Do not use the root user for the lab, and do not create long-term access keys. Step 5.2.3 signs in with aws login, which gives temporary credentials.
5.2.2. Install the tools Tool Version Check Git any git --version Node.js 24 (set in the repo’s .nvmrc) node --version pnpm 12 (the repo pins pnpm@12.8.1) pnpm --version AWS CLI v2, a version that has aws login aws --version Install pnpm after Node.js:
npm install -g pnpm@12 You do not need to install AWS CDK separately: the CDK CLI version is pinned in infra/package.json and always runs through pnpm --filter infra exec cdk. Docker is not needed either: TypeScript Lambdas are bundled with esbuild, and the Python Lambda only needs its files copied.
Get the source code and install dependencies:
git clone https://github.com/hhieuann/shop-ai.git cd shop-ai git checkout develop pnpm install 5.2.3. Sign in to AWS from your machine aws login The command opens a browser to sign in, then stores temporary credentials for the CLI. They expire after a few hours; when an AWS command says they expired, run aws login again.
Check that you are in the right account and set the default Region:
aws sts get-caller-identity --query Arn --output text aws configure set region ap-southeast-1 5.2.4. Bootstrap CDK CDK needs a CDKToolkit stack (a bucket for Lambda code and the deploy roles) in every Region it deploys to. The sandbox only uses ap-southeast-1. Run this in PowerShell from the repo root:
$acct = aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text; pnpm --filter infra exec cdk bootstrap "aws://$acct/ap-southeast-1" It ends with Environment aws://…/ap-southeast-1 bootstrapped. You only do this once per account.
The team’s prod environment also has AWS WAF. A web ACL attached to CloudFront must live in us-east-1, so the team’s account is bootstrapped in both Regions. The lab sandbox has no WAF, so skip us-east-1.
5.2.5. Create budget alerts Create budgets before deploying, so a forgotten resource sends you an email.
Open Billing and Cost Management → Budgets → Create budget. Choose Use a template → Monthly cost budget. Set Budgeted amount to 5, enter the email address for alerts, then Create budget. Repeat with 10 and 20 if you want several levels. AWS emails you when actual cost passes 85% and 100% of the amount, and when forecasted cost passes 100%. The team uses exactly these three budgets ($5, $10, $20) on the project account.
5.2.6. Create the HMAC key for behaviour data shop-ai does not store real userId values in the events table used for recommendations. A Lambda hashes userId with HMAC-SHA256 and a secret key stored in SSM Parameter Store at /shop/<environment>/events/hmac-key. The key is not in CDK (no secrets in source code), so you create it once by hand before deploying. The sandbox uses the sbx environment.
Check whether the key exists:
aws ssm describe-parameters --region ap-southeast-1 --parameter-filters "Key=Name,Values=/shop/sbx/events/hmac-key" --query "Parameters[].Name" --output text If the output is empty, create a random 32-byte key. The command does not print the key and clears the variable afterwards (PowerShell):
$k = [Convert]::ToBase64String([System.Security.Cryptography.RandomNumberGenerator]::GetBytes(32)); aws ssm put-parameter --region ap-southeast-1 --name /shop/sbx/events/hmac-key --type SecureString --value $k --query Version --output text; Remove-Variable k It prints 1 (the first version of the parameter).
Do not change the key on a running environment: the same user would hash to a different value and their past behaviour would no longer match. If you skip this step, ordering still works but the purchase event messages end up in a DLQ. Chapter 5.6.5 describes exactly this incident and how to fix it.
5.2.7. Cost How much does this lab cost? Close to $0. The lab sandbox has no WAF and creates no CloudWatch alarms (the two biggest costs in prod). Every other service is billed per use, and one person’s lab traffic fits within the Free Tier. Remember to do chapter 5.7 to delete the resources when you finish.
How much does a month of real use cost? The team built an estimate in AWS Pricing Calculator for “a small shop running in prod for one month”, using the configuration in the CDK code:
Estimate link: https://calculator.aws/#/estimate?id=0798eb584d82c280a557b96fbf3c8fbe695a6ca0
Traffic assumptions:
Assumption Value How Visits 30,000/month about 1,000 a day API requests 450,000/month 15 requests per visit: products, recommendations, cart, events CloudFront requests 1,050,000/month 35 requests per visit (API plus static files) Data out from CloudFront 50 GB/month about 1.5 MB per visit Orders, emails 300 orders, 600 emails confirmation and cancellation emails Signed-in users 2,000 MAU Result (Singapore, before tax):
Service Main configuration USD/month AWS WAF 1 web ACL, 2 rate-based rules + 3 managed rule groups, 1.05 million requests 10.63 Amazon CloudFront 50 GB out to the internet, 1.05 million HTTPS requests 7.32 Amazon CloudWatch 1 GB of logs (kept 2 weeks), 10 alarms, 1 dashboard, 5 custom metrics 3.21 AWS X-Ray 460,000 traces 2.34 Amazon DynamoDB On-demand, 0.2 million writes, 0.9 million reads, PITR 0.71 Amazon API Gateway HTTP API, 450,000 requests 0.56 Amazon SES 600 emails 0.06 Amazon S3 0.1 GB, 21,000 requests 0.02 Amazon Cognito Lite plan, 2,000 MAU 0.01 AWS Lambda Arm, 512 MB, 460,000 invocations, 150 ms 0.00 Amazon SQS, SNS, EventBridge Scheduler, SSM Parameter Store 0.00 Total 24.86 (298.32/year) The Calculator does not subtract the CloudFront Free Tier (1 TB and 10 million requests a month). At 50 GB and 1.05 million requests, the $7.32 is really $0. So the real cost is about $17.5/month, more than half of it WAF. There is no VPC, NAT gateway, EC2, RDS or load balancer, so there are no other fixed costs.
If you build the estimate yourself, watch out for three defaults that distort the result:
DynamoDB defaults to provisioned capacity (about $30/month plus $205 upfront). Turn it off and turn on on-demand capacity. Cognito defaults to Advanced security features on (about $100/month at 2,000 MAU). shop-ai does not use them; choose Disabled. SNS and EventBridge Scheduler default to “million per month”, and the fields do not accept decimals. Change the unit to “per month”, then enter 300 and 30. Compared with the real bill Cost Explorer for the team’s account, 01–15/11/2026, covering dev, staging and prod, before credits:
Service Real cost AWS WAF $1.27 (WAF on since 12/11, about $0.33/day, or about $10/month) AWS Cost Explorer $0.07 (Cost Explorer API calls) Amazon DynamoDB $0.07 Amazon API Gateway $0.04 Amazon S3 $0.02 Amazon SES, CloudFront under $0.01 Lambda, Cognito, SQS, SNS, CloudWatch, X-Ray $0 (within the Free Tier) The real numbers match the estimate: at demo traffic, WAF is almost the whole bill. The serverless services cost close to $0 because they are billed per use. The second item to watch is CloudWatch alarms: the three environments have 13 alarms, counted as 20 metrics (an alarm with metric math counts as 2), which is above the 10 free alarms and costs about $1/month. The team will remove WAF after the submission, following the runbook docs/runbooks/waf.md.
Preparation is done. Chapter 5.3 deploys the shop-ai infrastructure to your sandbox with CDK.

title: Deploying the Infrastructure
content:
This chapter deploys all of shop-ai to your sandbox with AWS CDK: one command creates the DynamoDB tables, Lambda functions, HTTP API, Cognito, queues, S3 bucket and CloudFront. You then open the web app, sign up, and check the security headers that CloudFront adds. The last two sections are further reading about things that exist only in the team’s environments: AWS WAF in prod, and CI/CD with GitHub Actions without access keys.
Goals Deploy the two stacks shop-sbx-<name>-api and shop-sbx-<name>-web. Open the web app through CloudFront, see the demo products, sign up and sign in. Understand how CloudFront splits requests between S3 and API Gateway, and which security headers it adds. Finish chapter 5.2 first: you have run aws login, bootstrapped CDK and created the HMAC key.
5.3.1. Choose a sandbox name Everyone has their own sandbox, identified by a short name made of lowercase letters and digits only (for example an, hoang). The name becomes the prefix of every stack: shop-sbx-<name>-api, shop-sbx-<name>-web. The commands below use an; replace it with your own name.
Every CDK command must include -c env=..., and a sandbox also needs -c owner=.... If either is missing, CDK stops immediately, so nobody deploys to dev, staging or prod by mistake.
5.3.2. Build the web app The web stack uploads apps/web/dist to S3, so build it first. From the repo root:
pnpm --filter web build If you forget, every CDK command stops with a message asking you to run pnpm --filter web build before synth or deploy.
5.3.3. Preview the changes pnpm --filter infra exec cdk diff --all -c env=sbx -c owner=an The command lists every resource that will be created; on the first run every line has [+]. Every synth also runs cdk-nag against the AWS Solutions rules. If a finding has no recorded justification, synth fails before anything is deployed.
The CDK app has two stacks:
Stack Contains Notes shop-sbx-an-api 7 DynamoDB tables, about 13 Lambda functions (Node.js 24, arm64), an HTTP API with a JWT authorizer, a Cognito user pool, SQS and DLQs, SNS, EventBridge Scheduler A custom resource SeedProducts loads 104 demo products into the products table shop-sbx-an-web An S3 bucket (public access blocked), CloudFront with Origin Access Control, a response headers policy, a config.json file Depends on the api stack: it needs the API URL and the user pool IDs 5.3.4. Deploy pnpm --filter infra exec cdk deploy --all -c env=sbx -c owner=an CDK shows the IAM permissions it will create and asks Do you wish to deploy these changes (y/n)?. Type y. The api stack deploys first, then the web stack, about 5 minutes in total; CloudFront alone takes a few minutes to push its configuration to the edge locations.
When it finishes, CDK prints the outputs. The two you need:
Outputs: shop-sbx-an-api.ApiUrl = https://xxxxxxxxxx.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com shop-sbx-an-web.WebUrl = https://dxxxxxxxxxxxxx.cloudfront.net Check in the console: CloudFormation → Stacks, type shop-sbx in the filter. Both stacks must be CREATE_COMPLETE.
To see the outputs later: CloudFormation → select the stack → Outputs tab. That tab also shows ARNs and queue URLs that contain your account ID, so hide them before sharing a screenshot.
5.3.5. Open the web app, sign up and sign in Open WebUrl in a browser. The home page shows the categories; Tất cả sản phẩm (All products) lists the 104 demo products that were just loaded.
Click Đăng ký (Sign up) and fill in Username, Email, Password (at least 8 characters) and Confirm password. Use an email address you can read: Cognito sends a verification code to it.
Enter the code, then sign in with the email and password you just created.
The web app has no Cognito settings built in. On load it reads /config.json (the web stack creates this file from the api stack’s outputs), then talks directly to Cognito using SRP: the password never passes through CloudFront or the API. The tokens it receives go with every API request, and API Gateway’s JWT authorizer checks them before calling a Lambda.
Cognito sends verification emails from the default AWS address, limited to about 50 emails a day per account, which is enough for the lab. Order confirmation emails are sent by SES, which the sandbox turns off (see the note in chapter 5.6.1).
5.3.6. CloudFront: one domain for the web app and the API The CloudFront distribution has three behaviors, matched in order:
Path Goes to Cache /api/v1/products* API Gateway 60 seconds, keyed by query string. The product list is the most called API /api/* API Gateway None. Cart, orders and events are per-user data default S3 (through Origin Access Control) Optimised for static files The web app and the API share one domain, so the browser does not need CORS. The S3 bucket blocks all public access; only this distribution can read it, through Origin Access Control.
Check the routing (replace with your WebUrl):
curl -s "https://dxxxxxxxxxxxxx.cloudfront.net/api/v1/products?limit=1" curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://dxxxxxxxxxxxxx.cloudfront.net/api/v1/me The first returns JSON with one product. The second returns 401: /me requires sign-in, and the JWT authorizer rejected a request without a token.
5.3.7. Security headers Every response from CloudFront goes through a response headers policy. See the real headers with:
curl -sI https://dxxxxxxxxxxxxx.cloudfront.net/ Result on the team’s sandbox (16/11/2026), unrelated lines removed:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK X-Frame-Options: DENY Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data: https:; font-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https://cognito-idp.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none' X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=() Header Effect Content-Security-Policy The browser only runs scripts and styles from this domain, with no 'unsafe-inline', so a script injected into the page (XSS) does not run. connect-src allows Cognito because the web app signs in directly with Cognito Strict-Transport-Security The browser uses only HTTPS for this site for one year. CloudFront also redirects http:// to https:// X-Frame-Options: DENY, frame-ancestors 'none' No site can embed the shop in an iframe, which prevents clickjacking X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff The browser does not guess file types Referrer-Policy Only the domain, not the full path, is sent when a user follows a link to another site Permissions-Policy Turns off camera, microphone, location and payment, which the shop does not use Adding these headers cut the OWASP ZAP scan from 12 warnings to 6 (chapter 5.6.6).
5.3.8. Further reading: AWS WAF in prod The sandbox, dev and staging have no WAF, to save money (a web ACL costs about $10/month, see 5.2.7). In prod a web ACL is attached to CloudFront with five rules, in order:
Priority Rule What it does 10 AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList Blocks IPs on AWS’s reputation list (bots, known attack sources) 20 RateLimitPerIp Blocks an IP that sends more than 1,000 requests in 5 minutes 30 RateLimitEventsPerIp For /api/v1/events only: more than 300 requests in 5 minutes is blocked, so nobody can flood fake events to skew recommendations 40 AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet General rules: XSS, path traversal, unusual request sizes 50 AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet Known attack patterns such as Log4Shell A web ACL for CloudFront must live in us-east-1, so WAF is a separate stack (shop-prd-waf) in that Region. CDK passes the web ACL ARN to the web stack with crossRegionReferences. WAF logs go to CloudWatch Logs, log group aws-waf-logs-shop-prd, kept for 14 days.
The common rule set can block legitimate requests, so the team first ran it in count mode. From the v1.0.0-rc.1 deploy (12/11) to 16/11 the logs had 678 requests and 0 blocks. The common rule set counted 74 requests, all of them the team’s own XSS test requests; no real request was wrongly matched. From v1.0.0 the rule set blocks.
5.3.9. Further reading: CI/CD with GitHub Actions and no access keys You deploy your sandbox from your own machine. The shared environments (dev, staging, prod) are deployed only by GitHub Actions:
Event Environment Condition Merge into develop dev automatic Push a release/* branch staging automatic Push a vX.Y.Z tag prod another team member must approve (GitHub environment production) After each deploy the workflow runs smoke tests, plus end-to-end tests on dev and staging.
GitHub stores no AWS access keys. Instead:
The job asks GitHub for an OIDC token signed for that run only. The job calls sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with the token and gets temporary credentials that last about an hour. The role’s trust policy matches the token’s sub field against the repository and GitHub environment. A job in the dev environment can only assume gh-deploy-dev; to use gh-deploy-prod the job must run in the production environment, which means someone approved it. A job running on a pull request can only assume gh-diff-readonly to run cdk diff, with no write access. The OIDC provider and the four roles are in infra/bootstrap/github-oidc.yaml, deployed once per account. One problem worth recording: GitHub repositories created after July 2026 use a new sub format that contains immutable IDs of the owner and the repository (repo:<owner>@<id>/<repo>@<id>:environment:dev), so a trust policy written for the old format fails with Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. The fix came from reading the real sub value in the CloudTrail AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity event.
The infrastructure is running. Chapter 5.4 walks through the sales flow: cart, ordering through SQS and confirmation emails.

Three lessons: the table-exists waiter only waits about 8 minutes; the new table does not carry over TTL, PITR, deletion protection or tags; pointing the application at the new table runs into IAM and IaC ownership. States clearly what was not drilled (copying data back, full RTO).

title: Testing and Operations
content:
In the previous chapters you deployed shop-ai and placed a test order. This chapter shows how to look inside the running system: follow one order through the logs, see the request path in X-Ray, know which alarm fires for which problem, and recover a message stuck in a dead-letter queue (DLQ). It ends with the team’s performance, recovery and security-scan numbers.
Everything below runs on your sandbox (shop-sbx-<name>) in ap-southeast-1.
Goals Find every log line of an order from a single ID. Read an X-Ray trace that goes through API Gateway, Lambda, SQS and DynamoDB. Know which alarms exist and which runbook each one points to. Move a message from a DLQ back to its source queue after fixing the cause. 5.6.1. Place an order to get data Open the sandbox web (output WebUrl of the shop-sbx-<name>-web stack) and sign in. Add 1 product to the cart and place an order with fake data, for example “Khách Test”, 0900000000, “1 Đường Test, Phường Test”, TP. Hồ Chí Minh. Do not cancel this order. Note the order ID shown on the order page (like 01M7H7MF…) and the time. Within 1–3 seconds the worker processes the queue message and the order moves from PENDING to CONFIRMED.
Check in DynamoDB: DynamoDB → Tables → table shop-sbx-<name>-api-OrdersTable… → Explore table items → Scan, add a filter orderId equal to the order ID, then Run. The order must have status = CONFIRMED; createdAt and updatedAt are a few seconds apart (the worker’s processing time).
The sandbox is deployed without -c senderEmail=..., so the worker does not send a confirmation email. This is intentional: Amazon SES in sandbox mode can only send to verified addresses.
5.6.2. Follow an order with CloudWatch Logs Insights Every request to API Gateway has a requestId. The ordering Lambda copies it into the SQS message as correlationId, and the worker logs it. So one ID finds every step of an order, even across different log groups.
Find the order’s correlationId: CloudWatch → Logs Insights, select log group shop-sbx-<name>-api-OrderProcessorLogs…, a time range around the order time, and run:
fields @timestamp, correlation_id, message | filter @message like /<order ID>/ The correlation_id column is the value you need (for example G6iL_hbgSQ0EJgw=).
Also select log group shop-sbx-<name>-api-ApiAccessLogs… (the API Gateway access log) and run:
fields @timestamp, service, routeKey, status, message | filter @message like /G6iL_hbgSQ0EJgw=/ | sort @timestamp asc The result has 2 rows in time order: API Gateway received POST /api/v1/orders and returned 201, then about 3 seconds later the order-processor worker logged “Đã xử lý tin đơn hàng” (order message processed).
The query selects only the fields worth reading. With the default @log, @message, the result shows the account ID (inside the log group name) and the caller’s IP; avoid that when taking screenshots or sharing results.
5.6.3. See the request path with AWS X-Ray Every shop-ai Lambda has X-Ray tracing on and wraps its AWS SDK clients, so each call to DynamoDB, SQS, SNS or SSM becomes a segment in the trace. X-Ray links traces across SQS into a set of linked traces.
Take the xray_trace_id from the worker log (the same line as correlation_id in the previous step). CloudWatch → X-Ray traces → Traces, paste the trace ID into the search box and open the trace. The map has 3 connected parts:
Client → ordering Lambda → DynamoDB (write the order, decrement stock) and SQS (message for the worker). Worker order-processor → DynamoDB (order to CONFIRMED) and SNS (order confirmed notification). Lambda events-purchase receives the SNS message through SQS → SSM (read the HMAC key) and DynamoDB (write the anonymised purchase event used for recommendations). Segments Timeline shows the time of each part; in this run the worker took 1.59 seconds because it was the first cold start.
5.6.4. Alarms and runbooks Alarms exist only in dev, staging and prod (not in sandboxes), because all three environments share one account and the 10 free alarms. Each alarm emails through SNS when it goes to ALARM and when it returns to OK, and has a runbook in docs/runbooks/.
Alarm Fires when Environments Runbook api-5xx The API returns 3 or more 5xx errors in 5 minutes dev, staging, prod api-5xx.md api-latency-p95 p95 above 1,000 ms for 3 consecutive 5-minute periods (only periods with at least 20 requests count, so a few cold starts do not fire it) dev, staging, prod api-latency.md presignup-errors Real errors in the sign-up check Lambda (rejections for a taken or invalid username are subtracted) dev, staging, prod lambda-errors.md orders-dlq A message is in the order queue’s DLQ prod dlq-orders.md order-enqueue-failed An order was saved but its message could not be sent to the worker prod dlq-orders.md lambda-throttles Lambda invocations are throttled by the concurrency limit prod lambda-throttle.md recs-pipeline-no-success The nightly recommendation job had no successful run in 26 hours prod recs-pipeline.md In November 2026 the 13 alarms (prod 7, staging 3, dev 3) used about 20 alarm metrics, because alarms with metric math count as 2, about $1/month above the 10 free alarms. The team keeps the dev and staging alarms to catch problems before prod.
5.6.5. A real incident: missing HMAC key, message in the DLQ The trial run of this lab on a new sandbox (16/11/2026) hit exactly one operational error, and it is a good example of what a DLQ is for.
Symptom: placing and cancelling orders works, but the events-purchase Lambda logs:
ERROR Không ghi được PURCHASE, SQS sẽ giao lại {"error": {"name": "ParameterNotFound", ...}} (could not write PURCHASE, SQS will redeliver)
Cause: the Lambda hashes userId with a key in SSM /shop/sbx/events/hmac-key. The key is created with the CLI and is deliberately not in the CDK template (no secrets in source code), so cdk deploy does not create it. The new account only had keys for dev, staging and prod.
What happened: SQS redelivered the message a few times, failed each time, then moved it to the DLQ OrderConfirmedEventsDeadLetterQueue. The message was not lost, only parked.
Fix:
Create a random key without printing it (this step is now in chapter 5.2):

title: Clean Up
content:
This last chapter deletes everything the lab created, so the account stops costing money. Most of it is one cdk destroy command, but a few things live outside the stacks and must be deleted by hand: log groups of the helper Lambdas that CDK generates, the HMAC key in Parameter Store, and the CDK bootstrap stack. The team found these leftovers when trying the lab on a fresh sandbox (16/11/2026).
Goals Delete the two sandbox stacks and confirm no DynamoDB table, S3 bucket, user pool or distribution remains. Delete the resources that live outside CloudFormation. Check Billing the next day for any remaining cost. The commands use the sandbox name an as in chapter 5.3; replace it with yours. Run aws login first.
5.7.1. Delete the two sandbox stacks From the repo root:
pnpm --filter infra exec cdk destroy --all -c env=sbx -c owner=an CDK asks Are you sure you want to delete: shop-sbx-an-web, shop-sbx-an-api (y/n)?. Type y. CDK deletes the web stack first (it uses the api stack’s outputs), then the api stack. CloudFront is the slowest step: the distribution has to be disabled at every edge location before it can be deleted. On the team’s sandbox (16/11/2026) the distribution alone took almost 3 minutes and the whole command about 5 minutes.
The sandbox is set up to delete cleanly, unlike prod:
Resource Sandbox, dev, staging Prod DynamoDB tables, Cognito user pool Deleted with the stack (RemovalPolicy.DESTROY) Kept (RETAIN); the user pool has deletion protection Web S3 bucket Emptied and deleted automatically (autoDeleteObjects) Kept Stacks Can be deleted right away Termination protection on So for a sandbox, cdk destroy also deletes the orders and user accounts you created in the lab.
5.7.2. Delete leftover log groups Every shop-ai Lambda has its log group declared in CDK, so it is deleted with the stack. The helper Lambdas that CDK generates (emptying the bucket before deletion, copying the web app to S3) are different: their log groups are created by Lambda on first run, outside CloudFormation, so they are not deleted. They look like:
/aws/lambda/shop-sbx-an-api-CustomS3AutoDeleteObjectsCustomRes-... /aws/lambda/shop-sbx-an-web-CustomS3AutoDeleteObjectsCustomRes-... /aws/lambda/shop-sbx-an-web-CustomCDKBucketDeployment... When trying the lab, the team found log groups from an 08/10 deploy still there, even though the sandbox had been destroyed and redeployed since. These log groups never expire. They are small and cost almost nothing, but delete them to keep the account clean.
List them:
aws logs describe-log-groups --region ap-southeast-1 --log-group-name-prefix /aws/lambda/shop-sbx-an- --query "logGroups[].logGroupName" --output text Delete them all (PowerShell):
(aws logs describe-log-groups --region ap-southeast-1 --log-group-name-prefix /aws/lambda/shop-sbx-an- --query "logGroups[].logGroupName" --output text) -split "\s+" | Where-Object { $_ } | ForEach-Object { aws logs delete-log-group --region ap-southeast-1 --log-group-name $_; "Deleted $_" } Run the list command again; the output must be empty.
On the team’s sandbox, the list command still showed 5 log groups after cdk destroy: 1 from the api stack and 4 from the web stack. Each time a stack is created again, the helper Lambdas get new names (a different random suffix) and write to new log groups, so the more often you deploy and destroy, the more log groups are left behind.
The prefix includes the sandbox name (shop-sbx-an-), so the command only deletes this sandbox’s log groups. Do not shorten it to /aws/lambda/shop-: in an account shared with the team, that would also delete the dev, staging and prod logs.
5.7.3. Delete the HMAC key You created the key by hand in chapter 5.2.6, so cdk destroy does not touch it. A standard SecureString parameter is free, but it is an unused secret, so delete it:
aws ssm delete-parameter --region ap-southeast-1 --name /shop/sbx/events/hmac-key If you deploy the sandbox again later, create a new key first (chapter 5.2.6).
5.7.4. Check nothing is left Check Command Expected CloudFormation stacks aws cloudformation list-stacks --region ap-southeast-1 --stack-status-filter CREATE_COMPLETE UPDATE_COMPLETE --query "StackSummaries[?starts_with(StackName,'shop-sbx-an')].StackName" --output text empty DynamoDB tables aws dynamodb list-tables --region ap-southeast-1 --query "TableNames[?starts_with(@,'shop-sbx-an')]" --output text empty S3 buckets aws s3api list-buckets --query "Buckets[?starts_with(Name,'shop-sbx-an')].Name" --output text empty Cognito user pools aws cognito-idp list-user-pools --region ap-southeast-1 --max-results 60 --query "UserPools[?starts_with(Name,'shop-sbx-an')].Name" --output text empty shop-ai Lambda log groups aws logs describe-log-groups --region ap-southeast-1 --log-group-name-prefix shop-sbx-an- --query "logGroups[].logGroupName" --output text empty Helper Lambda log groups the list command in 5.7.2 empty On the team’s sandbox, after 5.7.1 to 5.7.3, all six commands returned empty output. Also check in the console:
CloudFormation → Stacks, type shop-sbx-an in the filter, Filter status: Active: no stack is left. Switch to Deleted to see the two stacks as DELETE_COMPLETE.
CloudFront → Distributions: no distribution described as shop-ai web (sbx). The three that remain are dev, staging and prod, managed by GitHub Actions and not part of the lab.
The old WebUrl no longer opens: its *.cloudfront.net domain name was deleted with the distribution.
5.7.5. Delete the CDK bootstrap (if you no longer use CDK) The CDKToolkit stack from chapter 5.2.4 costs nothing when idle, apart from a few cents for the files in its bucket. If you still plan to use CDK in this account, keep it. Otherwise:
S3 → bucket cdk-hnb659fds-assets-<account>-ap-southeast-1 → Empty, type permanently delete to confirm. The bucket has versioning on; Empty also removes all old versions. CloudFormation → stack CDKToolkit → Delete. If the bucket is still there after the stack is deleted, go back to S3 and Delete it. If the account is shared with the team (dev, staging, prod), do not delete CDKToolkit: GitHub Actions needs it to deploy.
5.7.6. The next day: check Billing Billing data lags by about a day, so check the next day:
Billing and Cost Management → Cost Explorer, set the range from the lab day to today, Group by: Service. No lab service should show cost after the clean-up day. At one person’s lab traffic, the services usually stay within the Free Tier and show $0. Keep the budgets from chapter 5.2.5 for a few more weeks: if anything was left behind, AWS will email you. 5.7.7. Further reading: cleaning up the team’s environments after submission Prod is protected against accidental deletion (termination protection, tables and bucket set to RETAIN), so it is not cleaned up with a single cdk destroy. The team has a runbook, docs/runbooks/waf.md, section “Dọn sau khi nộp bài” (clean-up after submission), with two options:
Option A, remove only WAF (the team’s choice, because graders may still open the site until the internship ends): change the code so prod no longer creates the WAF stack, and deploy prod through the release process so CloudFront no longer has a web ACL. Then turn off termination protection, delete the shop-prd-waf stack in us-east-1 and the aws-waf-logs-shop-prd log group. WAF is the biggest cost (about $10/month). Option B, remove all of prod: note the web bucket name, delete the prod web stack and then the WAF stack, then delete the retained web bucket by hand. After this the prod site is gone. In both options the order matters: the WAF stack cannot be deleted while its web ACL is still attached to the distribution.
You have finished the lab: you prepared the account, deployed shop-ai, used it, observed the running system and cleaned everything up.

Reviewed and approved Nhân’s PR #294: the recommendations job now prints a single JSON line for Logs Insights; suggested adding the data check counts to the summary line. Approved the plan for an OWASP ZAP baseline scan (passive only) of the dev site for threat model C3 and L4: dev only, no AJAX spider, not during a deploy or on the release cut day. Checked Blog 1 before publishing: the sentence is fixed; the post and diagram do not expose the account ID; screenshots still need the account ID masked. Nhân’s ZAP baseline results (0 FAIL, 12 WARN, 56 PASS), checked the dev site headers myself: The “Server leaks version” warning is only Server: AmazonS3. The SRI warning comes from the Google Fonts link. COEP should not be enabled because it would block the fonts. Created issue #299 for a CloudFront response headers policy (L4) after v0.2.0, noting that the CSP must allow Cognito and Google Fonts. Reviewed, approved and merged Nhân’s PR #301: threat model L4 now rates the ZAP warnings correctly; SRI and COEP accepted with reasons. Fixed a bug Hoàng found while reviewing #289 (PR #303): signing out did not clear the recommendations cache, so the next person signing in on the same device briefly saw the previous user’s “Dành cho bạn”. Signing out now clears the recs cache, with a test that fails before the fix; approved by Hoàng and deployed to dev. Wednesday (28/10/2026) Worked at the office with Hoàng. Reviewed v0.2.0 progress and ran section 1 of the checklist early: dev deploy green; no open security alerts (Dependabot, CodeQL, secret scanning all 0); October cost by env tag close to zero. O7 acceptance on dev: read the worker logs and SES sending statistics (5 emails sent, 0 bounces); Hoàng confirmed receiving both the confirmation and cancellation emails. Split security work with Nhân: Nhân owns WAF end to end, I own C1 (blocking direct execute-api calls). Flagged WAF cost while not on the CloudFront Free plan, and that the WebACL must live in us-east-1. ListUsers permission of the pre sign-up Lambda (from a reviewed bug list): The Lambda could call ListUsers on every user pool, including prod since all environments share one account. Checked the Service Authorization Reference (the userpool resource supports aws:ResourceTag) and added an env tag condition. Verified the tag on all 4 real user pools; wrote a failing test before the fix; CI green, awaiting Nhân’s review. Thursday (29/10/2026) Merged PR #305 after both Hoàng and Nhân approved it: the pre sign-up Lambda can only call ListUsers on the user pool tagged with the same env. Checked after the dev deploy: Signing up with a new username works. Invoking the Lambda directly with a test event rejects a duplicate username (USERNAME_TAKEN). The IAM Policy Simulator on the real role allows the dev pool and denies the staging and prod pools. This also confirmed that the #280 metric filter counts the rejection and the alarm does not fire falsely. Nhân’s WAF proposal: according to the CloudFront flat-rate pricing plans docs, accounts on the AWS Free Tier cannot subscribe to a plan, so the free WAF approach of ADR-0006 is not possible. Decided on pay-as-you-go WAF on prod only (about $10/month, paid from credits); Nhân will update ADR-0006 in the WAF PR. Checked CDK bootstrap: CDKToolkit exists in us-east-1 and ap-southeast-1 (version 32), and the GitHub deploy roles can assume the us-east-1 roles, enough to put the WAF stack in us-east-1. Settled the final v0.2.0 scope: web view and add-to-cart events (R4) move to v1.0.0-rc.1 because Hoàng could not finish in time, tracked in issue #306. Updated the checklist (PR #308) to defer R4 and record O7 as passed on dev. Week 7 Achievements: Product recommendations working on dev: Nhân’s nightly job writes the recs table (first real run 27/10, no errors), the recommendations API returns data, and 2 web widgets (“Đang được mua nhiều” / “Dành cho bạn” on the home page, “Thường mua kèm” on the product page). Signing out also clears the previous user’s personal recommendations (#303). Ordering complete on dev: the worker confirms orders and sends emails through SES; O7 acceptance passed (Hoàng received both the confirmation and cancellation emails). Security: closed the OIDC review (#180, risk accepted with GitHub safeguards); fixed 2 false-positive alarms (#280); the pre sign-up Lambda can only read the user pool of its own environment (#305), verified with the IAM Policy Simulator; decided on pay-as-you-go WAF on prod only after finding that a Free Tier account cannot use the CloudFront Free plan. Agreed the v0.2.0 scope with the team: admin, WAF, the MFA screen and web events move to v1.0.0-rc.1; the acceptance checklist assigns each area to someone who did not build it. Not achieved: release/v0.2.0 was not cut on 30/10 as planned and moved to week 8. Blog 1 was fully reviewed but not published (account ID in screenshots still to be masked). Lesson: several PRs were merged without review early in the week; after a reminder, PRs later in the week all waited for approval before merging.

title: Week 8 Worklog
content: Week 8 Objectives: Release v0.2.0 (late from week 7): cut the release branch on 03/11, acceptance testing on staging 03–04/11, tag to prod on 05/11. Fix bugs found during acceptance, or record clearly that they move to v1.0.0-rc.1. Prepare v1.0.0-rc.1: WAF (Nhân), C1 and security headers (me), admin page, web events (Hoàng). Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material 3 - Reviewed progress, proposed a new schedule (tag 05/11, rc.1 12/11) - Merged checklist #308, cut release/v0.2.0, checked staging - Order acceptance O1–O8 on staging (PR #318) - Reviewed Nhân’s security report (#310), merged 4 Dependabot PRs - Ran the recommendations job on staging, pulled logs for S6 03/11/2026 03/11/2026 Test Lambda functions Workflow concurrency 4 - Reviewed Hoàng’s 4 PRs fixing #315, #316, corrected base branches - Recorded recommendation results R1–R3 (#348), opened #333 - Corrected my NEWEST mistake in #333 - Reviewed and merged #338, #340, #341; approved #344 - Measured Lighthouse on 3 dev pages, kept the target of 90 - Retested O5, #316 on staging; checked logs, X-Ray 04/11/2026 04/11/2026 Lighthouse X-Ray and SQS 5 - Reviewed and merged #350 (Nhân’s security checks S1–S6) - Brought the release into main (#357, #359, #361) - Tagged v0.2.0, prod deploy green at 12:41 - Checked prod: alarms, recommendations job, test order - Alarm recs-pipeline-no-success went to ALARM, then OK - Closed the checklist, brought fixes back to develop (#368) 05/11/2026 05/11/2026 CloudWatch alarms SES production access commitlint 6 - Closed the v0.2.0 checklist (#374), wrote the rc.1 checklist (#376) - Fixed the nightly run after enabling Schemathesis (#378, #383) - Deferred the ordering canary (#386) - Security headers for CloudFront (#388, issue #299) - Reviewed Nhân’s WAF (#372), 2 admin PRs (#385, #387) 06/11/2026 06/11/2026 Schemathesis CloudFront response headers MDN CSP Task details: Tuesday (03/11/2026) Reviewed progress after 4 days with no changes: v0.2.0 had not been branched or tagged; proposed a new schedule to the team: tag 05/11, v1.0.0-rc.1 moved to 12/11. Cut the release branch: merged checklist #308 and cut release/v0.2.0; staging deploy green (smoke test, E2E). Checked staging: the email worker has all environment variables, the recommendations schedule is enabled, the queue and DLQ are empty, 3 alarms OK. Order acceptance tests O1–O8 on staging: O1, O2, O3, O4, O6, O8 passed; O7 had passed on dev. O5 partly passed: the web does not show the guidance text and link when over 3 orders (#315). Also found that /orders does not redirect to sign-in when signed out (#316). Checked the worker logs; cancelled all test orders to restore stock. Recorded results in the checklist (PR #318 into the release branch). Reviewed Nhân’s draft security report (#310): merged #310 and 4 Dependabot PRs into develop, dev deploy green. Ran the recommendations job manually on staging so recommendation tests have data; pulled the PURCHASE Lambda log for Nhân’s S6 check (no personal data in logs). Wednesday (04/11/2026) Reviewed Hoàng’s 4 PRs fixing #315 and #316: found that #320 and #322 targeted the wrong base branches, and #320 would have pulled a batch of library updates from develop into the release. Corrected the bases, then merged #321 and #322 into the release and #320 into develop. Recommendations R1–R3: recorded Hoàng’s results in the checklist (#348). Opened #333 for the recommendation block title not following source, moved to v1.0.0-rc.1. Mistake: told Hoàng that staging returned NEWEST without calling the API; Nhân checked and found BESTSELLER, and I corrected it in #333. Product detail page: reviewed and merged Hoàng’s #338, #340, #341, resolving a tokens.css conflict. Approved #344, which fixes the panel table of contents. Lighthouse: measured 3 dev pages to compare with Hoàng’s numbers; Hoàng traced the difference to the Lighthouse version. Decided to keep the target of 90 and fix the method on dev CloudFront. Retested on staging: O5 passed; /orders redirects to sign-in and returns to the same page (#316). No unusual errors in 48 hours of logs; the queues and DLQ at 0; the dashboard has the queue charts. X-Ray: 2 consecutive traces (ordering sends to SQS, the worker has its own trace). Duplicate username metric: run for real on dev, configuration only on staging. Thursday (05/11/2026) Reviewed #350 (Nhân’s security results S1–S6): compared HTTP codes with the access log; asked for fixes to an extra table cell that hid the results column and a job note in the wrong order; merged after the fixes. Brought the release into main (#357): CI was red because commitlint flagged 2 old Dependabot commits of 102 characters, fixed in #359. The release branch lacked a commit from main and gh pr update-branch returned an error, so I connected them through #361 (no file changes). Hoàng approved and merged #357. Tagged v0.2.0: Nhân pressed Approve; prod deploy green at 12:41, smoke test 6/6. Updated the release note. Checked prod: The 3 new alarms exist. The recommendation block was empty because the job had not run, so I ran it manually and it wrote the bestsellers (NEWEST because prod has no orders yet, which exposes bug #333). Placed and cancelled 1 test order (O1, O2, O6): passed; emails were rejected as not_verified because SES is still in sandbox. Alarm recs-pipeline-no-success: went to ALARM at 12:46 because the previous 26 hours had no runs (Nhân explained this is by design) and returned to OK at 13:46. Closed out the release: closed the checklist, wrote the release lessons, and brought the fixes back to develop (#368; #366 had to be closed because its branch name contained a dot, against the rule). Friday (06/11/2026) Checklists: closed the remaining boxes of the v0.2.0 checklist (#374). Compared the plan with the code and wrote the v1.0.0-rc.1 checklist (#376): Branch cut 10/11, tag 12/11. In scope only the minimal admin API and screen, k6 load test, PITR drill and nightly fixes. Canary and the EC2 comparison deferred. Fixed the nightly run that went red after enabling Schemathesis (#378, #383): The contract was looser than the server, so I added patterns for ProductId, PageCursor, OrderId; added schemathesis.toml. Dropped checks that do not apply (CloudFront answers TRACE, API Gateway returns JSON for malformed URLs). Nightly green. Deferred the ordering canary (#386): set ADR-0014 to deferred and renamed the step in deploy-prod.yml, which had been named canary although prod deploys directly. Security headers for CloudFront (#388, issue #299): a ResponseHeadersPolicy with a CSP that only allows the site and Cognito, frame blocking, HSTS 365 days, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, and the Server header removed; applied to all 3 behaviours, live on dev. Reviewed and approved: #372 (Nhân’s WAF, revised after my feedback) and 2 of Hoàng’s admin PRs: order transition API (#385), Lambda and routes (#387). Week 8 Achievements: v0.2.0 in prod on 05/11: deploy green at 12:41, smoke test 6/6, release note published. This release brought queue-based ordering with confirmation emails, product recommendations and 3 new alarms to prod; the new product page is in rc.1. Acceptance on staging, with each area tested by someone who did not build it: orders O1–O8 passed after Hoàng fixed #315 and #316 on the release branch; recommendations R1–R3 passed; Nhân’s security checks S1–S6 passed, cross-checked with the access log. Operations on staging and prod verified: no unusual errors in 48 hours of logs, queues and DLQ at 0, X-Ray traces linked across SQS, and the recs-pipeline-no-success alarm returned to OK after the first run. Agreed the v1.0.0-rc.1 scope (cut 10/11, tag 12/11) and wrote the checklist: admin order transitions, WAF on prod, k6 load test, PITR drill; canary (ADR-0014) and the EC2 comparison deferred. Nightly now really runs ZAP and Schemathesis against staging and is green, after tightening the contract to match the server. CloudFront security headers (CSP, HSTS, frame blocking) are live on dev. Not achieved: the v0.2.0 tag was 3 days late against the 02/11 plan; on prod, emails to unverified customers are rejected because SES is still in sandbox; the recommendation title bug (#333) moved to rc.1. Lessons: settle what moves out at least 2 days before the cut; release fixes must branch from and target release/*; merge main into the release branch at cut time so the PR into main is not BEHIND; after the first deploy with a new job, run it once and check the page.

title: Week 9 Worklog
content: Week 9 Objectives: Finish the work due before cutting release/v1.0.0 (10/11): k6 load test, PITR restore drill, missing runbooks, checklist update. Acceptance testing of v1.0.0-rc.1 on staging 10–11/11, tag to prod on 12/11. Measure performance and recovery numbers (P1–P3) for the report. Decided 8 design points for admin order cancellation (BR-11) 12/11/2026 12/11/2026 PITR restore table-exists waiter WAF logging 6 - Ran the WAF Logs Insights query for Nhân’s check - Checked the first nightly recommendations job on prod - Admin acceptance on prod - Recorded sections 4–6 of the rc.1 checklist (#453) 13/11/2026 13/11/2026 WAF log fields Cognito TOTP MFA RFC 6238 Task details: Monday (09/11/2026) Merged #393 (Hoàng’s status in the rc.1 checklist) and #395 (k6 scripts): smoke.js runs nightly against staging through CloudFront. tiers.js measures 50 and 200 virtual users directly against API Gateway, with a place-then-cancel order path when E2E credentials are set. The new table has no TTL, PITR or deletion protection, as expected. Deleted the temporary table. Learned that even a 9 KB table takes several minutes, and the table-exists waiter only waits about 8 minutes. Checked Hoàng’s pre-check of admin AD1–AD3 on dev: deploy 9f9adf0 green, the 2 E2E 401/403 tests passed, the dev admin group only contains Hoàng’s account. Recorded as a pre-check because the author tested his own feature; the official acceptance is still on staging. Updated the rc.1 checklist (#403): Dev deploy green (E2E 46/46); nightly ZAP and Schemathesis green; no High Dependabot or CodeQL alerts; the release ruleset blocks branch deletion. Settled C1 (direct execute-api calls bypass WAF) with Nhân: recorded as a known limitation for rc.1. Checked Nhân’s reasons in the code: stage throttle 50/100, every write route has the JWT authorizer, event spam stays at 0.3–2% per the poisoning experiment. Recorded C1 and P1 in the checklist (#407). Dependabot: merged 3 PRs that do not touch running code (#397–#399); held #400 (17 web and Lambda libraries) until after the cut so rc.1 keeps the exact code measured for P1. Reviewed and approved Hoàng’s #405 (order page spec): checked it against the code; reminded him to open the 5 follow-up code PRs after the cut. Tuesday (10/11/2026) 09/11 nightly run: ZAP and Schemathesis green; k6 smoke ran for real for the first time, 73 requests, 0 failures, p95 823 ms (close to the 1000 ms threshold because staging Lambdas start cold at night). Cut release/v1.0.0 (ae8fcfa): merged main at cut time so the PR into main is not BEHIND. Verified the running code on the branch is identical to 9f9adf0 (the build measured for P1 and pre-checked for admin). Staging deploy green: smoke test, E2E. Reviewed Hoàng’s PRs: #409 (API returns firstItemName, the admin API keeps 5 fields through its own type) and #411 (Button, Badge, EmptyState, ConfirmDialog with tone); approved and merged them into develop after the cut, together with #400. Dev deploy green. Ran the recommendations job manually on staging: 104 products, all 3 recommendation types activated version 20261110 (ALSO_BOUGHT hit rate 0.54 vs. baseline 0.28), no errors in the log. P2 load test on staging: Reads: 50 virtual users p95 127 ms; 200 virtual users (36 requests/second) p95 108 ms; 0 failures, no throttling. Placed and cancelled 80 orders: p95 269 ms, 0 failures. Afterwards no open orders remained and the queues and DLQs were at 0. Staging E2E user’s password: did not remember it, so I set a new random password on Cognito and in the GitHub secret without showing it on screen; reran the staging deploy and the order E2E tests passed 9/9 with the new secret. Mistake: the first k6 command still had the placeholder <user E2E> and failed; the next one used the real values from the GitHub environment variables. Created my own staging admin account: enabled TOTP through the CLI, following the process agreed in threat model L5 (the web has no MFA setup screen yet). The first attempt failed with Missing required parameter PASSWORD because pasting the whole block made Read-Host read an empty line; running the blocks one at a time worked, and the account now has SOFTWARE_TOKEN_MFA. Admin acceptance AD1–AD3 on staging, passed: Moved an order CONFIRMED → SHIPPED → DELIVERED with a confirmation dialog each time and no way back. The customer sees “Đang giao” and the Cancel button is gone. A customer account opening /admin is told it has no permission; a signed-out visitor is sent to /login; the admin API returns 401 without a token. Security checks S1–S5 on staging, passed: another account viewing or cancelling A’s order gets 404; no token gets 401; a wrong price gets 409 PRICE_CHANGED with no order created; reusing an Idempotency-Key with a different body gets 422. Cancelled the test order; stock unchanged. Technical checks after acceptance: Queues and DLQs at 0; no errors in the metrics of 17 Lambdas. The logs only show not_verified email warnings (SES sandbox) and 2 TransactionConflictException errors when k6 cancelled orders right after placing them; SQS redelivered and processed them. Security headers present on all 3 CloudFront behaviours; a real sign-in with TOTP is not blocked by the CSP. Sent the team the day’s acceptance results and what is still pending (Hoàng R1–R3, Nhân W1–W3, E1). First bug fix into the release branch: reviewed and merged Hoàng’s #419 (issue #417, the “3 undelivered orders” message on the checkout page now uses the warning colour instead of the error colour, as documented). Checked that the branch came from release/v1.0.0, has a test that catches the bug, and CI is green; staging redeploy green. Asked Hoàng to retest R2. “Set up a cost budget using AWS Budgets” activity (Earn AWS credits, $20), 4th attempt: Chose Start activity and created a new budget “My Monthly Cost Budget” from the guided flow with tutorialId. Checked Hoàng’s R1–R3 results on staging: Test orders cancelled; queues and DLQs at 0; the 4th order blocked with the yellow message; recommendation APIs return the right source. Found that Hoàng still had 3 CONFIRMED orders left from R2, and that his repeated Lighthouse run did not state the environment (dev and staging now serve different web builds); asked him to cancel the orders and confirm where he measured. Checked Nhân’s W1–W3 and E1 results: The staging events table has VIEW and ADD_TO_CART at 20:03; userIdHash is a 64-character hash with no email or raw userId; ttl 90 days. The add-to-cart while signed out was not recorded because the route needs a JWT; a missing product returns 404. Confirmed his note that /favicon.ico returns 403 (S3 does not allow listing), left for after rc.1. By the end of the day every acceptance row in section 3 had passed; only tonight’s ZAP run is pending. Wednesday (11/11/2026) 10/11 nightly run against staging on the rc.1 build: ZAP 0 FAIL, 6 WARN (previously 12), 62 PASS; the warnings for missing CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Permissions-Policy and the Server header are gone thanks to #299. New warning “CSP: Wildcard Directive” from img-src https:, to tighten after rc.1. Schemathesis 2,893 cases passed; k6 smoke p95 783 ms. Lighthouse with Hoàng: confirmed his repeated run was on staging with the rc.1 build (643af49): 98 / 98 / 94, still passing. Checked he cancelled his 3 test orders; no open orders left on staging. Recorded all acceptance results in the rc.1 checklist (#429, issue #428): Section 2, AD1–AD3, W1–W3, E1, R1–R3, S1, P1–P3, technical checks, ZAP, bug #417. Changed tiers.js to print the Cognito error type when the E2E sign-in fails, tested with a fake client. Pushing one more commit after Hoàng approved dismissed his approval, so I asked him to approve again, then merged; staging redeploy green. Brought release/v1.0.0 into main (#430): Not BEHIND, because main was merged at cut time. CI failed the first time because the flaky HomePage test hit its 15-second timeout on the runner; the code was identical to a green run, so I reran the job and it passed. Asked Hoàng or Nhân to approve. #430 approved by Hoàng and Nhân and merged into main (ee4fd22). Verified main is identical to the release branch and that release/v1.0.0 still exists thanks to the deletion rule in the ruleset (v0.2.0 lost its branch). Sent the team the plan to tag v1.0.0-rc.1 to prod on 12/11. Earn AWS credits: the widget still shows 4 of 5 after the 4th attempt; prepared the text for an AWS Support case. Nhân’s issue #431 (favicon 403): index.html has no <link rel="icon"> and apps/web/public is empty, as described; to be fixed after rc.1 on develop. Forgot password for the release after v1.0.0 (answered Hoàng): Checked the user pool already has accountRecovery: EMAIL_ONLY and preventUserExistenceErrors. Decided: after the reset the user returns to /login with the email filled in; the default Cognito email template is kept; the documentation PR comes before the code. Found that threat model L1, L3 and L8 say “WAF rate limiting”, but the web calls cognito-idp directly so WAF does not apply; asked Nhân to fix them. Decided that if old refresh tokens still work after a password reset, signing out all devices is done right away (a Post confirmation trigger calling AdminUserGlobalSignOut, in a separate infra PR). Thursday (12/11/2026) Blog 2 “PITR is on, but have you tried restoring a DynamoDB table?” (posted on the AWS Study Group): Content: RPO/RTO; PITR always restores to a new table; real numbers from the 09/11 drill (23 = 23 items, 3–10 minutes, latest restorable time 4 min 59 s behind); three lessons. Checked every detail against the AWS documentation before posting: the table-exists waiter polls every 20 seconds, at most 25 times; the list of settings to set again after a restore; the AWS CLI merges pages for scan --select COUNT. Fixed an arrow in the diagram and renumbered the references. Updated the report’s Blogs section with the links to Blog 1 and Blog 2. Tagged v1.0.0-rc.1 on main (ee4fd22, the accepted build): prod deploy approved by Hoàng, green after about 5 minutes; first creation of the shop-prd-waf stack in us-east-1, shop-prd-api and shop-prd-web updated, smoke test green. Checked prod against section 6 of the checklist: Web ACL shop-prd-web attached to CloudFront, 5 rules (2 rate-limit rules blocking, the core rule set counting until about 15/11). WAF logging works, 15 test requests all ALLOW with no false matches. Product and recommendation APIs return 200; /orders and /admin/orders without a token return 401; all security headers present. The home recommendation block shows “Có thể bạn quan tâm” as expected when source is NEWEST; 7 prod alarms OK. GitHub Release: the auto-created release was not marked pre-release and showed as Latest. Wrote extra notes with “Fixes during acceptance” and “Not in this release” (Forgot password, MFA, favicon, CSP img-src, C1, core rule set in count mode, SES sandbox). Reviewed Hoàng’s #440 (Forgot password documentation): matches the 3 decisions; the threat model drops WAF from L1, L3, L8 and adds L9 (old sessions survive a password reset, with evidence from a dev test). Asked him to fix one contradictory line in dang-nhap.md and to note that L3 and the sign-out-other-devices criterion depend on L9. The first attempt returned Code mismatch because the 52-character secret was mistyped into the app. Wrote a PowerShell script that computes the TOTP code locally to compare with the app (checked against the RFC 6238 test vector); redid it and got SOFTWARE_TOKEN_MFA; the script never writes the secret to a file. Base layer: CloudFront + WAF is the only entry (static web on S3 via OAC, /api/* to the HTTP API, /api/v1/products* cached); Cognito issues JWTs checked by the HTTP API JWT authorizer; each module is one Lambda outside a VPC and one DynamoDB table (ADR-0005, 0006, 0007, 0012). Flow 1 browsing: catalog reads products, recommendation only reads precomputed results from the recs table; events stores VIEW, ADD_TO_CART with an HMAC-hashed userId and rejects PURCHASE from the browser. Flow 2 ordering: one DynamoDB transaction (price check, stock decrement, at most 3 open orders, write PENDING), then SQS; the worker sets CONFIRMED, publishes SNS order-confirmed so events records PURCHASE, sends the SES email; after 3 failures the message goes to the DLQ.
